title: Introduction
text: Introduction horizon-mods-lib is a library of native mods for Horizon , the free, open-source rewrite of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 in Rust. Every mod is its own small project with its own tests, its own release and its own .hnmod file. They are ports: each one re-implements something people already use in Fabric (a FPS readout, a zoom, a key overlay, waypoints) on Horizon's native hook points. What a native mod is A Fabric mod is Java that gets loaded into the JVM. A Horizon native mod is Rust source that horizon-mixins merges into the game's own source before it is compiled. The launcher builds a game for the instance the mod is installed in, so the mod is not a plugin loaded at run time: it is part of the executable you play. That has consequences, and this library is built around them: A mod can only do what the game's source lets it hook. Horizon keeps a short list of stable hook points (see Hook points ); mods written against them build on any Horizon whose hook-point version is new enough. A native mod runs with the player's rights, so the registry reads the source of every native mod before it lists it. These projects are small on purpose: a mod's logic is one runtime.rs file with unit tests, and each hook is a helper of a few lines. Everything is MIT, nothing is minified, and the .hnmod contains exactly the .rs and .toml files you can read in the repository. title: Install a mod
text: Install a mod Native mods are built into your game, so installing one means building one. The first build downloads Rust and can take 20 to 30 minutes; later builds are faster ( Horizon's native mods guide has the measured numbers). The quick way: all of them at once One download has every mod, unpacked and ready to build: curl -LO https://github.com/pxdns/horizon-mods-lib/releases/download/all-mods/horizon-mods-all.zip curl -LO https://github.com/pxdns/horizon-mods-lib/releases/download/all-mods/horizon-mods-all.zip.sha256 sha256sum -c horizon-mods-all.zip.sha256 unzip horizon-mods-all.zip -d horizon-mods && cd horizon-mods ./install.sh MyInstance # Windows: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File install.ps1 MyInstance install.sh asks you to type yes (these are native mods: source compiled into your game, running with your rights) and then runs horizon-launcher native-build ./mods --instance MyInstance --trust-native-code . The zip is rebuilt on every change to a mod, so the link above is always the newest. The README.txt inside lists what is in it, and says how to leave a mod out: delete its folder under mods/ before you build. Two pairs overlap, so use one of each: zoomify and simple-zoom both ask for a zoom (the first to answer wins), and freelook and freecam both take over mouse look and the camera. Everything in the zip was checked together on one Horizon commit. Want only some? Use the steps below. 1. Get the .hnmod Every mod has a GitHub release named -v with the .hnmod and its SHA-256 next to it. Download both and check the hash: sha256sum -c zoomify_1.0.0.hnmod.sha256 The tag and file name are zoomify-v1.0.0 and zoomify-1.0.0.hnmod ; the hash file names the exact file it covers. 2. Unpack it A .hnmod is a zip: horizon-native.json and mixins/ /… with the sources. Unpack it into its own folder: mkdir zoomify && cd zoomify && unzip ../zoomify-1.0.0.hnmod Read the files first. That is the point of a source-only bundle: runtime.rs is the whole logic, the other .rs files are one hook each. 3. Build it into your game Native mods are experimental in Horizon and the launcher asks you to trust the code. From the command line: horizon-launcher native-build ./zoomify --instance MyInstance --trust-native-code The folder can hold one unpacked bundle or several, so you can build a set of mods into one game. The launcher builds on the Horizon commit the mods name, or on the commit of the version you play when the mods name none. All mods in one build must agree on that commit; mods that use only the hook points (these all do) do not pin one. 4. Switch it on In the game, open Options → Mods . Each mod has a row with its description, a settings page and, where it has keys (the two zoom mods), the keys listed first. Getting it into the launcher's browser The launcher's Mods page lists what is in horizon-rust/horizon-mods , after a maintainer has read the source. These projects are not listed there unless their maintainers submitted them; read that repository's MOD-POLICY.md before doing so.

title: Build from source
text: Build from source You need Rust, Python 3.12+ and Git. The mods' own logic builds and tests with plain cargo ; checking them against Horizon needs Horizon's source and a few system libraries. Test a mod's logic cd mods/zoomify cargo fmt --check cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings cargo test --locked The Cargo library of each project is mixins/ /runtime.rs , the same file that horizon-mixins merges into the game, so what you test is what ships. Apply and type-check on Horizon tools/mods.py is adapted from the registry's own tool ( horizon-rust/horizon-mods , native/tools/native.py , MIT): python3 tools/mods.py list # every project python3 tools/mods.py check zoomify # apply on the pinned Horizon, cargo check the game python3 tools/mods.py check all # every mod together, as a player's set is python3 tools/mods.py package zoomify # target/zoomify-1.0.0.hnmod and its SHA-256 check downloads Horizon's source at the commit in compatibility.json (GitHub's archive, never a checkout), builds horizon-mixins at its pinned commit, applies the mods and runs cargo check on the modded game with warnings denied. On Ubuntu the game's crates need libasound2-dev libudev-dev libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev pkg-config . Pins compatibility.json in each project names the Horizon commit it was tested on and the horizon-mixins commit it was applied with, and "hooks": 1 : the hook-point API version it needs. See Compatibility .

title: Hook points
text: Hook points The hook points are empty functions in Horizon's crates/horizon-client/src/game/native_hooks.rs . The game calls them at fixed places; a native mod hooks them with HEAD injections. They keep their names and signatures from release to release and are only ever added; each addition raises NATIVE_HOOKS_API (3 at the commit these projects were tested on). Hook Called These projects use it for native_frame(elapsed) Once a frame Nothing yet native_tick() Once a tick, in every Game (check native_window() ) info-hud : speed from how far you moved native_world_lifecycle(…) World open, open failed, final close (API 3) Nothing yet native_hud(batch, corners) The HUD, not under F1 Every HUD mod: corners.place a box, draw with native_fill and native_text native_key(key, pressed) A key or mouse button, by vanilla name zoomify , simple-zoom native_wheel(steps, claimed) Wheel steps while playing The zoom mods claim them while zoomed native_command(command, ran) A chat command, before the server sees it /fps , /wp , /hud … native_zoom(zoom) Each frame while playing The zoom mods set factor, smoothing and turn scale native_minimap(minimap) Each frame Nothing here; Horizon ships a minimap native_mods(mods) Options → Mods lists native mods Every mod pushes its row native_settings(mod_id, buttons) A mod's settings page opens Every mod pushes its buttons native_settings_click(mod_id, button) A button was clicked Every mod flips its option native_panel_event(…) The item panel's clicks (API 2) Nothing yet Helpers the game gives a mod native_on , native_playing , native_window , native_corner_shown , native_text_width , native_fill , native_text , native_player (position, yaw, pitch, dimension), native_frame_rate , native_clicks , native_mapping , native_mod_key , native_chat , native_data_dir , native_setting , native_set_setting , and the item and recipe helpers of API 2. Reading the game's own state Some mods here ( armor-hud , potion-counter , totem-counter , effect-timer , apple-skin , pick-up-notifier ) hang on the stable native_hud and native_tick hook points, but they read what those hooks do not hand over: the inventory, armor slots, active effects and food, straight from Horizon's Game struct. horizon-mixins puts a mod's helpers inside Horizon's game module, where those private fields are visible. That works, and tools/mods.py check proves it compiles against the pinned commit, but it is not covered by the hook-point contract : if Horizon renames a field, these mods stop compiling and must be updated. For that reason they carry no hooks entry in compatibility.json , only the Horizon commit they were tested on. Hooking Horizon's own functions Four mods go one step further and use horizon-mixins' cancellable HEAD hooks on functions that are not hook points at all: freelook and freecam on perspective::turn_player (the mouse turns the view, not the player) and perspective::camera_view (the camera the frame renders from, run again with the mod's own angles); better-hurt-cam on fov::bob_matrix (the hurt and bob pose, rebuilt with a weaker tilt); and snappy-tappy and freecam edit the game's held-key set before movement is read. All four are pinned to the commit they were checked on. One thing mixins cannot do: rewrite a function that uses ? or closures except with a HEAD hook, which is why InvMove (it needs a change inside Horizon's tick function) is not ported. Chat and tooltips Chat and tooltips are Horizon's own code too. chat-notify , more-chat-history and chat-animation put their module in Horizon's chat file ( crates/horizon-client-render/src/chat.rs ) and hook Chat::add_message (before the original, and, for more-chat-history , instead of it with a longer limit), Chat::add_lines (a constant modified) and Chat::layout (rebuilt with a slide). durability-tooltip adds a RETURN modifier to stack_tooltip . title: Anatomy of a mod
text: Anatomy of a mod mods/zoomify/ Cargo.toml the Cargo library: points at runtime.rs Cargo.lock compatibility.json pinned Horizon and horizon-mixins commits, hooks API LICENSE README.md mixins/zoomify/ horizon-mixin.toml module + HEAD injections runtime.rs logic, state and tests (one file) key.rs wheel.rs zoom.rs one helper per hook list.rs settings.rs click.rs the Options > Mods row and page horizon-mixin.toml Declares one module (the file runtime.rs , added to the game's game.rs as game::lib_ ) and one injection per hook: [[module]] id = "runtime" file = "crates/horizon-client/src/game.rs" name = "lib_zoomify" source = "runtime.rs" [[injection]] id = "wheel" kind = "HEAD" target = "horizon_client::game::native_hooks::Game ::native_wheel" helper = "wheel.rs" bindings = [ { name = "game", ty = "&crate::game::Game ", value = "&*self" }, { name = "steps", ty = "f32", value = "steps" }, { name = "claimed", ty = "&mut bool", value = "&mut *claimed" }, ] A HEAD injection runs the helper before the hook point's own body, which is empty. Helper names are prefixed with the mod's id ( zoomify_wheel ) because every mod in a build ends up in the same module. runtime.rs Pure logic: no game types. It holds the mod's state in a thread_local! , reads settings through a closure the helper passes in ( |k| game.native_setting(ID, k) ), and carries its unit tests. That is what makes a native mod testable without the game. The helpers Each helper is a few lines: check game.native_on(ID) , read what it needs from the game, call into runtime.rs , draw or store the result. A mod that is switched off in Options → Mods does nothing until the next build leaves it out, so every helper checks first. compatibility.json and the manifest tools/mods.py package writes horizon-native.json into the .hnmod from compatibility.json : {"schema": 1, "id": "zoomify", "version": "1.0.0", "game": "26.3", "horizon": "ba6344a59cb9e755b730dcf02285fc0d33b97d3c", "mixins": "d9c83d7096b7ea5b83678da2efdfd6161f74997e", "hooks": 1} The launcher validates it ( schema 1 , exact 40-character revisions, hooks not zero) before it builds anything and refuses bundles with links, absolute paths or more than 512 entries.

title: Settings and storage
text: Settings and storage A native mod keeps its settings in files, one file per key, in horizon-mods/.horizon-mod-data/ / next to the game's options. game.native_setting(id, key) reads one (trimmed), game.native_set_setting(id, key, value) writes one. These projects store booleans as true and false ; anything else reads as the option's default. Zoom mods also store level (one of 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16). Waypoints stores every waypoint in one file called waypoints , one tab-separated line each ( name x y z dimension ); a line that does not read is skipped, not fatal. Keys are different: they belong to the game's controls. A mod lists keys in its Options → Mods row ( keys in NativeMod : name, label, default) and reads the player's choice with native_mod_key . Both zoom mods list one key. State that is not a setting (the zoom while it is on, the last position for speed, the tracked waypoint) lives in a thread_local! in runtime.rs and is gone when the game closes.

title: Releases
text: Releases Every project releases itself. Change the mod, and bump version in mods/ /mixins/ /horizon-mixin.toml (and Cargo.toml ). Push to main . .github/workflows/release- .yml calls the shared _release.yml , which runs cargo fmt --check , clippy with warnings denied and cargo test , packages the .hnmod , uploads it as a workflow artifact and, if the tag -v does not exist yet , creates that GitHub release with the .hnmod and a .sha256 file. A push that does not change a mod's folder does not trigger its workflow, and a push that does not change the version releases nothing. To test and package without releasing, run a workflow by hand from the Actions tab and leave publish off. ci.yml runs on every push and pull request: each mod's tests in a matrix, and a job that applies all mods on the pinned Horizon and type-checks the game, so a hook that no longer matches Horizon fails there and not on a player's machine. Versioning Semantic versions, per mod. A change that needs a newer hook-point API also bumps hooks in compatibility.json . A new Horizon commit is tested by changing horizon_revision (in compatibility.json and horizon-mixin.toml ) and letting CI apply the set.

title: DMCA and takedowns
text: DMCA and takedowns This library re-implements the behaviour of other people's mods. If you think a project here copies your work, or that something else in this repository infringes a right you hold, you can have it looked at and, if you are right, removed. How to send a notice Open an issue at pxdns/horizon-mods-lib titled DMCA notice , or, if you prefer not to post publicly, message the repository owner pxdns through their GitHub profile and ask for a private channel. GitHub also takes notices directly under its own DMCA policy , which applies to this repository whatever is done here. A notice should have the elements the law asks for (17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(3)): Your name and a way to contact you. The work you say is infringed, with a link to it. The material here you say infringes, with the file path or URL (a line range helps). A statement that you believe in good faith that the use is not authorised by the owner, its agent or the law. A statement that the information in the notice is accurate and, under penalty of perjury, that you are the owner or authorised to act for the owner. Your physical or electronic signature. What happens next The material is reviewed within a few days. If it is infringing, or if there is real doubt, it is removed from main and from the site, the release asset is deleted, and the project's page says so. Where the complaint is that a port is too close to the original, the fix may be a rewrite rather than a removal; you will be told which. Counter-notice If something was taken down and you believe that was a mistake, send a counter-notice by the same route with your name, contact details, the material removed and where it was, a statement under penalty of perjury that you believe in good faith it was removed by mistake or misidentification, and your consent to the jurisdiction of the federal court for your address (or, outside the US, any judicial district in which GitHub may be found), and your signature. title: Security
text: Security A native mod is native code with the player's rights. That is true of every native Horizon mod, and the launcher says so in red before it builds one. What this library does about it: Source only. A .hnmod contains .rs , .toml , a LICENSE and horizon-native.json , nothing compiled. You can read all of it, and the launcher checks the bundle without running anything. Small by design. Each mod's logic is one file with unit tests; the helpers are a few lines each. There is no unsafe , no network access, no process spawning and no dependency in any Cargo.toml . The only files a mod touches are its own settings files through native_set_setting . Reproducible. The .hnmod is packaged deterministically (fixed timestamps, sorted entries), so the same commit gives the same SHA-256, which the release publishes beside the file. Pinned. compatibility.json names exact commits of Horizon and horizon-mixins, never a branch or a tag. If you find a vulnerability, open a private security advisory on the repository (Security tab → Report a vulnerability) rather than a public issue.

title: Contributing
text: Contributing Ports are welcome. A good one is small, tested, and honest about what the hook points let it do. Pick a mod that fits the hook points. The catalogue marks what needs a hook point and what does not; if a mod needs one, the useful contribution is a pull request to Horizon that adds the hook point. Copy a project folder under mods/ and rename it ( slug for the folder, snake_case for the id). Keep runtime.rs pure, put the tests in it, keep each helper a few lines. Write it from behaviour. Do not copy or translate upstream code. See Licensing . Run cargo fmt , cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings , cargo test --locked , and python3 tools/mods.py check . Add a release- .yml (copy an existing one and change the slug), a row in docs/credits.md , and an icon in assets/icons/ . Open the pull request. CI applies all mods on the pinned Horizon. Everything under mods/ , docs/ , catalogue/ and the release workflows is generated from tools/gen/ : edit the generator and run python3 tools/gen/regen.py (it downloads the pinned Horizon source itself, and a second run changes nothing). See tools/gen/README.md . Be accurate in README claims: say what the mod does and what it does not, and name the upstream mod and its licence.

title: Home
text: Your favourite mods, rewritten in Rust. Horizon is a rewrite of Minecraft: Java in Rust, and its mods are not plugins: they are source that gets merged into the game and compiled with it. This is a library of them. 30 are done, each one a tiny project with its own tests, its own release and a file you can read in five minutes. Download all 30 mods Play Horizon See the mods Install guide How a Fabric mod becomes Rust 30 mods shipped 152 unit tests across them 0 dependencies in any mod 141 of 186 catalogued mods have a 26.3 build A mod is part of the game, not a guest in it Fabric loads Java into a running JVM. Horizon has no JVM. A native mod is Rust that horizon-mixins merges into Horizon's source before the compiler sees it, and the launcher builds a game for your instance with the mods already inside. Hook Horizon keeps a short list of stable hook points: empty functions the game calls every frame, tick, key press, HUD draw. Merge A horizon-mixin.toml says which hook runs which helper, and adds the mod's runtime.rs to the game as a module. Build The launcher compiles the modded source for your instance. First build 20 to 30 minutes, later ones faster. Play Switch the mod on or off in Options, Mods. It has a settings page and, if it needs one, a key. The 30 mods Each folder in mods/ is a complete project: logic, tests, pins, licence, a release workflow. They are ports, written from how the originals behave and not from their code. title: Why native mods
text: Why native Mods you can read, test and trust. A plugin system is a promise that code you did not read will behave. Horizon's native mods make a smaller promise and keep it: the bundle is source, and the source is short. There is nothing to load A Fabric mod is a jar the game opens at start-up, patches with bytecode tricks and runs inside the same JVM. Horizon is native Rust, so a mod cannot be loaded that way, and does not need to be. horizon-mixins works on the game's source tree: it parses the Rust, applies the injections a mod declares, and the compiler sees one program. A hook is a function call that was written into the game before it was built. No reflection, no class loader, nothing that decides at run time what runs. The bundle is the source A .hnmod is a zip of .rs and .toml files and a licence. Nothing compiled is in it. The launcher checks it without running anything, refuses links, odd paths and anything beyond the bundle layout, and then builds it for your instance behind a red warning, because native code has the player's rights. Horizon's registry lists a native mod only after a maintainer has read its source. You can do the same in the time it takes to drink a coffee: here, a mod's logic is one file of a few hundred lines at most. Logic that does not need the game to test Each project's Cargo library is its runtime.rs . The game's types never appear in it; the hook helpers read what they need and pass plain values in. That is why a zoom's wheel limits, a waypoint's bearing maths and a speedometer's smoothing have unit tests that run in under a second, and why a bug in them is a failed test instead of a crashed game. Small on purpose There are no dependencies in any of these projects. There is no unsafe , no network access and no process spawning. A mod that is switched off in Options does nothing at all until the next build leaves it out. Settings are one file per key in the mod's own folder. What it costs Build time. Every set of mods is a build of the game: the first one downloads a toolchain and takes 20 to 30 minutes, a rebuild of one changed helper takes a few minutes. Reach. A native mod can only do what a hook point allows. Servers. Native mods are not built for dedicated servers yet; on a server you join, only client-side hooks do anything. Maturity. Native mods are experimental in Horizon. We say so on every page that matters. See how a port goes The hook points

title: From Fabric to Horizon
text: Porting From Fabric to Horizon, one behaviour at a time. The Tempest project has a matrix of 186 Fabric mods across five game versions. This is what happens when you take that list to a game written in Rust. Start with the list Horizon implements Minecraft 26.3, so the first filter is blunt: 45 of the 186 mods have no 26.3 build and are out. Of the remaining 141, most are libraries, performance mods a native engine does not need, or packs. What is left is a short list of mods that are about what you see and press. Ported 24 Partly ported 6 Needs a hook point 15 Pack or asset 30 Engine or server 32 Library 28 No 26.3 build 45 Rule one: copy the behaviour, never the code Upstream mods are LGPL, GPL, MIT, all-rights-reserved. A port that contains none of their code owes them credit and nothing else, and it owes the reader an honest account of what it does. So each port starts from using the original, writing down what it does, and writing Rust. The credits name every original and its licence. Rule two: the logic gets tests Zoomify's wheel clamps between 1.25x and 16x. A test fails if it does not. Waypoints compute a vanilla yaw to a block; one test pins north, south, east and west. The hook helpers cannot be tested without the game, so they are kept to a few lines, and CI type-checks them against the real Horizon. Rule three: say what is missing Xaero's minimap is only partly ported: Horizon ships its own minimap, and there is no map-screen hook, so what is left is the waypoints idea. The catalogue says so. A port, end to end Zoomify holds a key and zooms. On Horizon that is three hooks. The key hook is this much code: // The zoom key went down or up: the player's own choice of key. fn zoomify_key(game: &mut crate::game::Game , key: &str, pressed: bool) { use crate::game::lib_zoomify as m; // Turned off in Options > Mods: nothing until the next build leaves it out. if !game.native_on(m::ID) { return; } if key != game.native_mod_key(m::ID, m::KEY, m::DEFAULT_KEY) { return; } let playing = game.native_playing(); let game = &*game; m::key(playing, pressed, |name| game.native_setting(m::ID, name)); } And the wheel claims its steps while the zoom is on, so the hotbar does not move: // While the zoom is on, the wheel changes it instead of moving the hotbar. fn zoomify_wheel(game: &crate::game::Game , steps: f32, claimed: &mut bool) { use crate::game::lib_zoomify as m; if game.native_on(m::ID) && m::wheel(steps) { *claimed = true; } } Everything else (the levels, the easing flag, the turn scaling, the settings buttons) lives in runtime.rs and has seven tests.

title: Trust
text: Trust Built so that you do not have to take our word. A native mod runs with your rights. Here is everything this library does about that, and what it asks of you. Source, not binaries A .hnmod holds Rust and TOML. Read it before you build it; the launcher validates it without running anything. Pinned and reproducible Exact Horizon and horizon-mixins commits in every project. The package is deterministic: same commit, same SHA-256, published beside the file. Clean-room ports Written from behaviour. No upstream code, art or text, and the credits name every original and its licence. Icons, credited Catalogue icons are each mod's own, from Modrinth, named to their authors on every page and gone on request. The nine projects have their own drawn icons. Nothing phones home No network access in any mod, no dependencies, no analytics on this site, no third-party fonts or scripts. A way to say stop If something here is yours and should not be, the DMCA page says how to ask, and what happens next. The honest limits. This is an unofficial project, not endorsed by the Horizon project, Mojang or Microsoft. Native mods are experimental in Horizon. The mods are unit-tested and type-checked against Horizon in CI, and have not been played through a real window by CI. Read the security notes and the disclaimer .

title: Roadmap
text: Roadmap What is waiting on Horizon, not on us. 15 catalogued mods cannot be written yet. The reason is never effort: it is that a hook point does not exist. Hook points are only ever added, so each one that lands unblocks a group of them. 1 mods Chooses entity textures by rules per entity; Horizon's mob renderers have no hook for that choice. [ETF] Entity Texture Features… 1 mods Replaces the Statistics screen, which Horizon draws and handles in `stats_screen.rs` (about 500 lines); a mod could only replace it whole. Better Statistics Screen… 1 mods Changes which texture a block face uses, inside the chunk mesher; there is no hook there. BetterGrassify… 1 mods Needs each sender's skin drawn beside chat lines; the chat has no skin access, and the HUD sprite atlas cannot take a player's head. Chat Heads… 1 mods Merges XP orbs in the entity simulation: entity logic, not something a hook point reaches. Clumps… 1 mods Changes the Controls screen, which Horizon builds in its generic options UI with no hook for a search box. Controlling… 1 mods Adds buttons to the crafting grid screen; the container screens have no hook for extra widgets. Crafting Tweaks… 1 mods Highlights slots in the inventory screen; there is no hook in the slot drawing. Item Highlighter… 1 mods Schematic loading, rendering and placement: a large feature, not something a hook-sized mod covers. Litematica… 1 mods Removes an end crystal on the client before the server confirms; it needs hooks in entity and packet handling. Marlow's Crystal Optimizer… 1 mods Adds a second binding per action to the Controls screen and the key map; both sit in Horizon's options UI, with no hook. Multi Key Bindings… 1 mods Predicts an ender pearl on the client before the server confirms; it needs hooks in entity and packet handling. Pearl Optimizer… 1 mods Adds a search box to the Statistics screen, which Horizon draws and handles in `stats_screen.rs`; there is no hook for a text field there. Search Stats… 1 mods Looks players up on an external tier service and draws the result on name tags; there is no network or name-tag hook. Tiers… 1 mods Adds a keyboard screen to the options; there is no hook for a new screen. VisualKeys… How a hook point gets added It is a change to Horizon, not to a mod: an empty function the game calls at a fixed place, a bump of NATIVE_HOOKS_API , and an entry in native-hooks.json . The most useful contribution this library can make is a pull request to horizon-rust/horizon that adds one, with a mod here that uses it. Hook points today Contributing

title: Play
text: Play Horizon in your browser. A full build of Horizon with its game files included: open it and it runs, with the game data served from this same site. It needs a browser with WebGPU. Play Horizon (offline) Download the file Horizon (offline) The page (1.3 MB) plus its wasm and resource package in horizon-offline/ (about 115 MB, fetched from this site only). horizon-offline.html · SHA-256 880c76c1b13b69f7d48ce537a5315fc4d51e505a5d8a631646bbe5c3cf010df3 How it starts Open the file It asks for a folder of game resources: the one that contains boot.tar.gz , manifest.txt and the res folder. Select it Your browser may ask you to confirm an upload; per the page, nothing leaves your computer. The resources are saved in this browser the first time, so you pick the folder once. Choose what to keep You pick what is saved in the browser (sounds are optional; only UK English is kept). Game saves are kept in the browser too. What it needs WebGPU. The file says so itself when it cannot find one. It runs in Chrome and Edge 113 or later on Windows, macOS and ChromeOS; Chrome 121 or later on Android; Safari 26 on macOS, iOS and iPadOS; and Firefox 141 or later on Windows. On Linux, Chrome, Edge and Brave need WebGPU switched on with --enable-unsafe-webgpu --enable-features=Vulkan . What to know You bring the resources. The file contains none of Minecraft's resources: the game reads the folder you select, which you prepare from your own copy of Minecraft. No mods built in. The mods in this library are compiled into a game by Horizon's launcher ( install guide ); this single file is a separate build, so do not expect them in it. Unofficial. This site is a community project; Horizon is not approved by or associated with Mojang or Microsoft. Horizon is MIT licensed. See credits for what the file's own comments name, and the disclaimer .
